catalog_quote: 2.3 Stress. In KN stress is not phonemic; it does not show semantic contrast. All words are regularly stressed as follows: the stress falls on the first syllable of one-syllable words: One-syllable words jóm 'hit' íd 'man' nóg 'go'. With two- and three-syllable words, (unless there is a long vowel) the stress falls on the penultimate. two-syllable words: dógir 'devil' jágin 'push' térig 'deaf' gútti 'kick'; three-syllable words: kašránge 'a plant' jagá:de 'wet' kilílle 'cry of joy' kanísse 'dough'. [p.22] A long syllable is always stressed: gillí:t 'organ' kerrí:t 'yogurt' iccí:n 'scorpion'. There are a few bisyllabic words that are stressed on the final syllable rather than the penultimate as predicted; such words are marked for stress in the lexicon: affí 'boy' kofré 'a plant' uffé 'blow'.

The footnote affirms that Andaandi (Dongolawi) has word stress, that the acute accent in Armbruster (1960, 1965) and Massenbach (1961, 1962) marks that stress rather than tone, that tone has never been investigated, and (secondhand, citing Massenbach 1961: 242) that the stressed/unstressed distinction carries little meaning, i.e. stress has a low functional load. The paper itself is a syntax paper with no phonology section.

new_statements.identity_note: Glottolog kenu1236 'Kenuzi-Dongola' covers two varieties: Kunuz/Kenzi Nubian (Mattoki; Egypt; ISO xnz), which Abdel-Hafiz's grammar describes, and Dongolawi/Andaandi (Sudan; ISO dgl; Glottolog dialect node dong1288), which Jakobi & El-Guzuuli 2016 and the works they cite (Armbruster 1960/1965, Massenbach 1961/1962) describe. The stress remark quoted is about Andaandi (Dongolawi), not Kenzi.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Kunuz (Kenzi) Nubian stress is non-phonemic and predictable: monosyllables are stressed; in two- and three-syllable words stress falls on the penult unless the word contains a long vowel, in which case the long syllable takes the stress wherever it is (gillí:t, kerrí:t, iccí:n final; jagá:de penult); a few disyllables are lexically marked for final stress (affí, kofré, uffé). Nothing is said about words of four or more syllables or about words with two long vowels.
new_statements.secondary_stress: not mentioned in sect. 2.3 (no secondary or rhythmic stress described).
new_statements.exceptions: (1) 'A long syllable is always stressed': long-vowel syllables override the penult default (gillí:t 'organ', kerrí:t 'yogurt', iccí:n 'scorpion'). (2) 'a few bisyllabic words.. stressed on the final syllable rather than the penultimate as predicted; such words are marked for stress in the lexicon': affí 'boy', kofré 'a plant', uffé 'blow'.
new_statements.identity_note: Abdel-Hafiz describes Kunuz (Kenzi, KN) Nubian as spoken in Egypt (Aswan region), i.e. the Kenzi half of Glottolog's Kenuzi-Dongola; the Dongolawi/Andaandi half (Sudan) is covered by Armbruster 1960, Massenbach 1961 and Jakobi & El-Guzuuli 2016, not by this work.
